## Design

### 2026-10-12 – ## Oct 12: Frame design and layout

**3h**

## Oct 12: Frame design and layout

I've been interested in mechanical clocks for a while, as we have a non-functional grandfather clock at home. I looked around the internet, and found some really interesting designs on [Thingiverse](https://www.thingiverse.com/thing:328569) and [MakerWorld](https://makerworld.com/en/models/1242934-mechanical-clock#profileId-1263783). I decided it could be challenging, but fun and practical to try and make my own, obviously a bit less ambitious than some of the other ones out there, but the same concept, with exposed gears, pendulum, and everything else.

After installing and opening Fusion, it was quite a lot. It took me a good moment to create the project and familiarize myself with the controls. I worked with Autodesk Inventor a little bit at school, so I knew absolute basics, but Fusion had quite a few nuances. At first, I realized I would need a frame for the clock, so I started sketching a 250 by 180 milimeter front plate, which should hopefully leave enough space for gears. I made it 4 milimeters thick for now, but I'm not sure if it'll be enough for the gears and the pendulum, so when those are finalized, I may need to reconsider it.

![Front plate](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/f06df9cbb946384b0f8e0606d83d40fdd1ec3ade85d2ff126512189b81c7f048.png)

Afterwards, I decided to start making holes in the front plate. The most obvious one was for the clock hands to go through in the center. I decided to look at the reference on Thingiverse, but counted a lot of shafts, which would be very difficult for this project. For now, I decided to go with five holes for now, four for the gears and one for the hands of the clock. This may mean that the clock will run for a shorter time before needing to be wound, but it's my first bigger project in CAD, and a sacrifice I am willing to make. I decided to place one hole in the center and 4 other holes around it positioned proportionally.

![Holes in the front plate](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/e9d98ebfbe0e9093160a434dfb1e31697955a4d6333f9d4017034165d38f07f8.png)

To make the gears visible while the clock operates, I made it a bit more open by adding rectangular windows.

![preview](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/dc5e0eda6c03e4d9dd14a9197c5c58a1ba6026b12b4108c8101802623a47b634.png)

For the back plate of the clock, I figured it would be easiest to simply duplicate front plate. I did so, and moved it 50mm back on the Z axis, where all the gears and mechanisms will live.

However, from my references, I noticed that the clock's pendulum generally hangs behind and below the frame, which would mean that the back plate would block it from swinging. Therefore, I made the back plate open at the bottom to let the pendulum rod move freely. I also rounded the top corners of the slot with filleting to make it a bit more aesthetically pleasing.

![Pendulum hole](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/494b2d3f0e25495225fb26a8bb776ff8bbaec0c88d763fc506ada0a67a168241.png)

To finish off the plates and the base of the clock, I added four cylindrical standoff posts at the frame corners. I drew 4 circles on the inner face of the front frame with a 12mm diameter and extruded them to 46mm length (50mm gap of the two plates minus the 4mm back plate thickness), which makes them sit flush against the back plate.

![Base of the clock](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/5bf7c6489fd2bc5227c220027a01c30b062d6730b6305e1e3a60b2162caa4045.png)

I'm quite proud of the base of the clock. It already looks like something, and tomorrow, I will start on the actual gear train.

 **tl;dr: Built the base of the clock, two frames, connected by standoff posts, added decorative windows, fileted everything and added holes for the gears and clock hands.**

**Total time spent: ~3 hours**

**Next up: Figuring out gear ratios and modelling the first gears**

### 2026-10-13 – ## Oct 13: Gear ratios and the gear train

**5h**

## Oct 13: Gear ratios and the gear train
Before I could even work in Fusion today, I had to figure out the gear ratios. The whole point of the clock is that the minute hand turns exactly once per hour, so the entire train of gears has to reduce the speed of the fastest gear down to one revolution.

I decided that this is going to be a wall mounted clock (like the references in my previous journal entry were), and because of that, I decided to go with about a 1 meter long pendulum, which should have a period of about 2 seconds (1 tick per second), simplifying the math quite a bit. Each tick of the pendulum advances the escape wheel (the first one) by one tooth, so with a 30 tooth escape wheel, it completes a full turn every 30 seconds, which comes out to 120 revolutions per hour.

The minute hand needs to do 1 revolution per hour (to match the minute hand), so the total gear reduction from the escape wheel (first wheel) needs to be 120:1. I decided to make three stages. In the first one, I went with a 4:1 ratio (40 tooth wheel driving a 10 tooth pinion), in the second stage I went with 5:1 (50 tooth wheel driving a 10 tooth pinion) and in the third stage, I went with a 6:1 ratio (60 tooth wheel driving a 10 tooth pinion).

Multiplying the ratio out comes to 4x5x6=120, which is the exact ratio we needed.

For the power input, I needed a great wheel which would hold all the energy for the clock when it is wound. I added a 60 teeth great wheel driving a 10 tooth pinion, giving another 6:1 reduction. The great wheel connects to the winding mechanism, and since it will turn once every 6 hours, the clock should (theoretically!) run for a few days between winds.

To generate the gears, I figured out that Fusion has a built-in script (SpurGear), which I used to generate each gear. After doing the math, the gear generation was relatively simple, as I needed to input a few parameters (tooth count, thickness, etc.) and I got a full gear. Much much easier than sketching gears by hand.

![Spur gear addon in Fusion](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/972a4911b8d797c2afe399fc5a24fcfb244744dc1e7d4c73222aedb0a1e250e4.png)

I started by generating the Great Wheel to get a feel for how the addon works, but didn't do much positioning until all the gears were generated, as I wasn't sure how they were going to fit.

![Generated great wheel](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/c00fa38dec1f586259fb46e501d25187b55ad62b6e36b5fea6e076a15f741d73.png)

In total, I generated 9 gears. The 60T Great Wheel, 10T Center Pinion and 40T Center Wheel, 10T Third Pinion and 50T Third Wheel, 10T Fourth Pinion and 60T Fourth Wheel and a 10T Escape Pinion with a 30T Escape Wheel.

Each shaft needs a pinion (a smaller gear receiving power from the last stage) and a wheel (big gear passing power to the next stage in the clock). I stacked them at different depths, to make sure they wouldn't collide.

![The gear train](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/f674d95e97f9c2df0ba57da2d4449f4c002682c7da0d080598b9fd8df3e68ab7.png)

**However, despite the fact that all was going  much better than I hoped, an avalanche of issues was about to start!**
When I originally placed the shaft holes yesterday, I mostly eyeballed them and placed them around proportionally in a way that looked right. However, now, I had actual gears with different tooth counts, so I needed to fix the positioning of the holes. I found that the center-to-center distance formula between two gears is (teeth1 + teeth2) * module / 2, so I used that to recalculate the shaft positions and edited the sketch to match.

![Fixing the shaft positions](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/80580bb91e79495ee328b80c2be399e30d083bcdc9d0d59ed5a4ab92aac13bc2.png)

This was really annoying, but if I didn't do it, the gears wouldn't mesh together and the whole clock couldn't work.

After placing some of the gears, I had some concerns that they weren't properly positioned, so I ran Fusion's interference detector, and found several collisions. Some gears were just barely too close, and the teeth would clip into each other. I had to move the shaft holes and individual shafts by fractions of a millimeter and rotate a few pinions, so the teeth slotted instead of colliding. This took a few rounds, but I was able to get to a no interference result.

![Interference detections](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/711bfe058098b793d465d8791d7fe79e43ca3a8a6c92cb65dbd5000580fad1cf.png)

I also added a new shaft hole for the escapement anchor, positioned above the escape wheel. Tomorrow, I will be working on the anchor, which is likely to be the most complex part.

![Today's progress](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/448a428491ea31d87828290a7284d968a7590f377b7416ab89bf1bb19541f969.png)

 **tl;dr: Worked out gear ratios, made all 9 gears using Fusion's SpurGear, repositioned yesterday's shaft holes and fixed interferences.**

**Total time spent: ~5 hours**

**Next up: Escapement anchor and pendulum**

### 2026-10-14 – # Oct 14: Gear ratio corrections, gear train redo, escapement and pendulum

**6h**

# Oct 14: Gear ratio corrections, gear train redo, escapement and pendulum
To begin the day, I made a rather detrimental discovery. My gear ratio calculation had a significant error. Originally, I thought that my goal ratio was 120:1, however, I realized that the escape wheel of the gear train advanced one tooth per full pendulum swing (I accounted for half). This means that with a 30 tooth escape wheel and a pendulum that swings once per second, it does one revolution every minute, which is obviously 60 rph, not 120. This meant that the gear train would only need a 60:1 reduction and not the 120:1 I built yesterday...

Obviously, this meant that I had to redo the gears. Another discovery was that the gears were placed a bit incorrectly and would overlap other parts of the clock (yesterday's interference passed, so I assumed it was fine, but the relevant parts haven't been built yet). Unfortunately, this meant I had to redo essentially all of yesterday's work. Knowing what to do, it was thankfully quite faster. My new ratio is 50/10 x 40/10 x 36/12 which comes out to the 60:1 goal ratio. I deleted all the gears from yesterday and recreated them with Fusion's SpurGear script and repositioned accordingly. Naturally, yesterday's issues repeated and we had interference between wheels and pinions, so I had to rotate each pinion slightly to make the teeth of the gears align.

![Interference result](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/3589c07f7f6abf7e699aecb7d087fd3f79fef9edb8f5d91fc79b18908f835c54.png)

I also had to remove one of the decorative windows from the front and back plate, as it overlapped with one of the new hole positions.

![The gear train without the escape gear (for now)](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/a48eee500e91188a3732bd9dcf426772483edf4c2d7c0d42691d973c71add655.png)

![Repositioned shaft holes and redesigned front/back plates](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/ad7b212224b5e2e4232e6f55feafefdf3e7d23f04e2bb2349100efcc41e4072e.png)

With the proper gear train, I started to work on the escapement mechanism of the clock. It was definitely the hardest part so far (but I might regret those words later..). I ended up creating a gear with specially shaped teeth to which the anchor could lock and release one at a time.

![Escapement anchor and escape wheel](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/af3b339e47eab837517d3f64577b02ba6b0a2db25ac509840a3135e77625bb7e.png)

Next up was assembling the pendulum. I started with the suspension bracket on the outer side of the back plate. It was a very simple sketch, just a small rectangle with a circle in it (a pin that sticks out) and the pendulum rod will hang on. The pendulum crutch was next, it's a flat arm that hangs down and has a small pin at the bottom. I realized it would be really useful to use Fusion's offset planes here, and they made the job a lot easier. The pendulum rod was almost a meter long, which suddenly made the model massive. Despite the actual mechanism of the clock being small and compact, the rod has to be long. And lastly, I placed a pendulum bob near the bottom of the rod, which can adjust the clock's speed.

![Upper part of the pendulum](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/13b8adfd26b09527464d1dfce90d72034cc249cccfa5c1f31ec979f67c4710b9.png)

![View on the entire clock with the pendulum visible](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/3b4647c10251e399d299feae4f05e9457c330cdb450576c5b0391218b97a1922.png)

**tl;dr: Fixed the gear ratio, rebuilt the entire gear train (most of yesterday's work), created the escapement, and assembled the full pendulum mechanism.**

**Total time spent: ~6 hours**

**Next up: Winding mechanism and motion for the hour hand**

### 2026-10-15 – # Oct 15: Axles, winding and optimizing the model

**5h**

# Oct 15: Axles, winding and optimizing the model
I realized I forgot to mention this in my past journal entries, but I've decided to make my clock wall mounted instead of the original plan for it to be a desk clock. The pendulum is almost a meter long, which.. wouldn't be so practical for a desk clock, unless your desk is very high and you don't mind drilling a hole into it. Wall clocks also generally have a longer runtime, and with a 20mm winding drum and a meter of drop, I think we can run for several days between winds. That's about as long as my antique grandfather clock that I have at home runs!

I recalled that in my PCB project, I ran into significant cost issues at Tier 2 and I had to barely scrape by with a lot of trade-offs during the last days, so I started thinking about material cost early. Since I don't have a printer, I'll need to get it printed by someone, which will possibly slightly inflate the cost, especially at Tier 1. I decided to shrink the frame plates from 250mm to 200mm, as the mechanism doesn't need that much space and there was useless material on the right side. I needed to delete one of the decorative windows again and reposition the standoffs, which also caused some collision issues, but I got it sorted out.

![Size comparison of the shortened vs longer plates](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/d831b87203898fcc5d9969fb3117e258ca30737bdad0c99667309836f052534b.png)

Next I made the bearing holes a little bigger, from 6mm to 6.4mm which gave the axles some extra clearance, so that they can freely rotate once printed. I modeled the axles themselves afterwards. The center axle extends 35mm out the front plate for the clock hands, and the great axle extends 15mm for the winding key.

![Overhanging axles](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/fe072c83c276189710988ab0374ed036df411bf2ae1c41efe3539836a67ee9ed.png)

I also added spacer hubs around each axle and joined each wheel to its pinion so that they can rotate together. It took me a little while to figure out how to join them, as the way SpurGear plugin made the gears made them a bit hard to work with.

![Spacer hubs around the axles](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/ac1ac1f0fd2c06e4d41cda7a6d4ee7eb08b8e466585055984248945e710d0b5f.png)

Unfortunately, just like I did yesterday, I made another detrimental discovery. The minute hand would run backwards with the current arrangement of gears. Every mesh reverses the direction of rotation, and an odd number of meshes between the escapement and center shaft would cause the hands to go counter-clockwise. Thankfully, the fix was much easier than yesterday, I just had mirror the escape wheel and anchor, which would flip the entire escapement mechanism.

Probably the biggest task today was the winding mechanism. I carved out a part of the center of the Great Wheel and put the winding ratchet inside. The ratchet is on the winging drum's axle, and two flexible click arms are part of the Great Wheel itself. When I wind it, the clicks flex out and slip over the teeth of the ratchet.

![The ratchet and click arms inside the Great Wheel](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/ff1a8ab23847c25a54eeb99bbe83077de8826ae9ec259f27efd3f32e4d09c315.png)

To finalize today's work, I made a spool-shaped drum for the winding mechanism.

![Winding mechanism drum](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/5cebb755c409363238d790cd9ea1e8632eb0b36fc476ab5f2e9bcbb6ef4d0793.png)

**tl;dr: Optimized for material cost, added axles and spacer hubs, fixed backwards rotation, built the complete winding mechanism.**

**Total time spent: ~5 hours**

**Next up:** Working motion and the dial

### 2026-10-16 – # Oct 16: Motion works, dial and hands

**4h**

# Oct 16: Motion works, dial and hands
So, today I mostly worked on the front plate of the clock and the clock face.

The center shaft turns once an hour, which is exactly what the minute hand needs, but 12 times faster than what we need for the hour hand. To fix it, I made a small gear train in front of the front plate. I used 10/30 and 8/32 gears, which together give a 12:1 ratio. The cannon pinion is located on the center shaft, the minute wheel and pinion on a small stud above it and the hour wheel is on a pipe around the cannon pinion.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/23d6ea4daacc8fbea4fa34be3a2e59c6cafd3dc51f4fe999fffe01369179b121.png)

The pipes were a bit of a mess, because my extruding would often select the wrong part and join into it or became a separate body, which I quickly noticed when checking interference. I had to redo them many times and merge them with the combine tool. It is really easy to make mistakes at this stage, as there are many components and selecting the wrong one can have very bad and often annoying to fix results.

![Finished pipes](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/dc95a7f70b3d3492976c7415c48e48508d0b907e3c8295cd39dec399fe2a8858.png)

The dial was paradoxically a bit easier, since it was just a circle with a few holes which I made with a circle pattern. I made 12 hour slots and stood it on 4 pillars that are in the front plate. I also didn't make it solid to make the mechanism behind it visible.

![Clock dial](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/966c2fc8089cb951c1f649a0c839a86336962ee7e59f803322c423b1cbde61c8.png)

To finish off the day, I made the hands for the dial and added a small collet on the tip of the axle to keep them from sliding off.

![Dial with the clock hands](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/e2e4a63ac45bb18828de13a1ff441675f328d35dc0c2e36642efeb7825c5fa28.png)

**tl;dr: Built the 12:1 conversion for the hour hand, the dial and the clock hands. The clock now has a complete face.**

**Total time spent: ~4 hours**

**Next up:** Final details and motion testing

### 2026-10-17 – # Oct 17: Final details: cord anchor, regulation, winding and wall mount

**4h**

# Oct 17: Final details: cord anchor, regulation, winding and wall mount

Even though the clock face and the mechanism was functional, the clock still wouldn't be properly usable without today's work. I needed to make the clock actually hangable, windable and make it possible to regulate it.

Firstly, I worked on the cord anchor. The drive weight will hang on a cord wrapped around the winding drum, but the cord had nothing to attach to, so I added a 2 milimeter hole on the left side where the weight will hang. Essentially, I will push one end of the cord through the small hole at the edge of the rear flange, knot it on the back side of the flange, wrap it around the drum  and the other end will come off the drum on the left side of the clock, dropping straight down between the two plates exiting out the bottom of the clock. I'm not yet sure how much of a weight I will need, I am estimating 1-3 kilograms, and I will likely use sand or water bottles when it is time to build it, but that's something to consider during the build week.

![Cord anchor](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/486b705b38c2457aa4bd488bd4fe44fc4e225ac64650277d24fcf88b36cecf46.png)

Next, I needed to make it possible to regulate the pendulum. Pendulum clocks are regulated by moving the bob up or down, so we cannot just fix the bob in one place. I did a bit of recalculating, moved the bob down 16mm, lengthened the rod and added an M8 threaded stud at the bottom. Now, the bob should slide on the rod and rest on an M8 nut which can be turned to move the bob, changing the clock's speed. My grandfather clock which I have at home works in a similar way, and if it is too fast or too slow, it can be adjusted.

![The pendulum bob](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/4340359b3c7d8654385cf424a023ada6bfc791d3bd484d22f4395ec1888235de.png)

Now, the winding key. Obviously the clock needs to be wound to insert potential energy into the system. The great axle was already sticking out the front, but it couldn't be gripped. So I added a small knob which will get glued at the end and sit in front of the hands.

![knob](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/a5fe59b89e6b87066500ba24797f795e7153b2acce38794a2c48630337113632.png)

Lastly, the wall mount. The clock will need to stand off the wall, so I added four feet on the back plate. The top two have keyhole slots, into which one can insert screw heads that are inside the wall. The bottom two feet have no slots and just rest against the wall.

![legs](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/a8248db5113511e2b9eeae46b3fcebf45f433b4e17c962eb6b9b521ad8102e78.png)

With this, I can proudly say my clock design is complete. It can be hung, wound and regulated at the bob. What's left is testing the motion, basic testing inside CAD and making sure that everything will properly work when built.

**tl;dr: Added a cord anchor to the drum, nut to regulate the pendulum at the bob, winding knob and wall-mount feet. The design should be complete.**

**Total time spent: ~4 hours**

**Next up: Motion testing and finalization**

### 2026-10-17 – # Oct 17 (v2): Making the clock actually buildable

**6h**

# Oct 17 (v2): Making the clock actually buildable

I said the design was already complete in my last entry, but turns out that was very premature celebration. I tried to see if each part of the clock is actually printable and buildable, and I was in for an unpleasant surprise, there were many problems that would make it impossible to build it properly. I suppose even in CAD, the famous rule that "the first 90 percent of a project account for the first 90 percent of its development time, whereas the remaining 10 percent account for the other 90 percent of the development time" also applies.

To be honest, today's work was very exhausting as I worked on this much longer than I hoped, but let's walk through it once more. The first issue was almost embarrassing, nothing actually held the two plates together. The standoffs were just cylinders sitting between the plates, so I added 8 M3 countersunk screws, one through each plate into each end of the four standoffs and the standoffs got 2.5mm holes.

![Screw holes](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/dddbd53c01b84b9134959ef2decad749f0220abec2008b595d6bdc0d644b2f4a.png)

Next was the escapement. Whether the escape anchor will grip the wheel properly depends on the distance, and if my print comes out a little off, the anchor could either jam or slip. To make it adjustable, I put the anchor axle in bushings. There is a small printed sleeve in both plates whose bearing hole is off-center by 1 milimeter, thanks to which turning a bushing moves the anchor up to 1mm closer to or further from the escape wheel. Once it is ticking properly, I will lock it in with a bit of glue.

![Bushings](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/761c29871937558f8f56dd8592a4f8c90a475949d8679491efc2d3ad53b732ed.png)

The biggest change was definitely the pendulum, as it had to be entirely remade. The previous design was too long to be printable and too specific to buy, so I redesigned it as a plain 1 meter threaded rod which I can use uncut. I will screw it into a printed top piece which also has the crutch slot. The rod will thread into the plastic and will be held by a nut. Keep in mind that the rod shown in CAD isn't accurate to how the real one looks (it is threaded in real life).

![Redesigned pendulum](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/80ab6f3f4df6ac5f8764baaf55791e9c397916d669d8dbe66f593bb3b193d8f0.png)

I also realized that a printed bob would likely be too light. So I redesigned it as a hollow 100 milimeter shape which will get filled with sand and closed with a printed lid. That way, it will be heavier and I also put nuts at the bottom to hold it and regulate it.

![Redesigned bob](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/ed3880613d9d1a5475600a3897535cc89ee3a0689559adb367290c3901545cac.png)

To make sure that my holes are accurate when I'm printing, I parametrized the relevant hole sizes and made a small test strip with 7 holes (for the axles and rods). During building, I will first print the test strip and see which holes fit to potentially change the parameters and account for tolerances.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/0fd25d2c90c68af2125178ac6e04e4a45c7df3d432fcc65ddeeb10b3532ff937.png)

I also did some more smaller fixes related to printing, mostly for the Great Wheel which would be unprintable due to gaps that are too small for a 3D printer. Also the suspension bracket would originally have to be glued onto the back plate, which would mean that the entire pendulum would be carried by a glued joint. So I joined it into the back plate instead which means it'll get printed alongside it. I also had to shrink the dial's opening from 56mm to 40mm to make sure the minute wheel doesn't slide off. This sadly means less of the mechanism is visible.

![Redesigned great wheel from the front](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/7770134c38b749f296126cc5b34d9f4861a96a81a62f6487c3475bfad0ff6228.png)

![Redesigned dial](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/f131e8d2848b12c06b84608049e399d2ac7f8166ec0783d9c2a144c5d78bad37.png)

**tl;dr: Fixed printability and buildability issues, such as plate screws, adjustable escapement, redesigned pendulum, sand-filled bob, parametrization with a test strip for tolerances**

**Total time spent: ~6 hours**

**Next up: Project submission**
